title: [v0.5.3] Lifecycle: secure upgrades, recovery and deprecation
author: mcpdev80
body:
## Goal

Make BaseHarbor upgrades predictable and recoverable while keeping the normal developer workflow simple.

> **A safe upgrade should feel boring.**
>
> **As little as possible, as much as necessary.**

## Upgrade model

```text
resolve current version/state
        ↓
preflight compatibility
        ↓
create recovery point where required
        ↓
migrate / upgrade
        ↓
verify
        ↓
READY or actionable recovery state
```

Do not report upgrade success before relevant post-upgrade verification succeeds.

## Scope

- upgrade compatibility preflight;
- deterministic migration ordering;
- recovery point/backup where a change can put durable state at risk;
- post-upgrade verification;
- rollback when technically safe;
- explicit recovery instructions when rollback is not safe;
- deprecation warnings;
- supported legacy-reading behavior;
- writer behavior that prefers the current canonical form;
- removal rules tied to explicit contract-version changes.

## Deprecation rules

Preferred model:

```text
compatible legacy input
   -> continue reading
   -> warn when useful/actionable
   -> write canonical current form
   -> remove only through documented breaking-version policy
```

Do not create warning noise for users who cannot or need not act.

## Developer experience

- normal patch/minor upgrades should not require a runbook;
- preflight catches incompatibility before mutation;
- errors say exactly what blocks the upgrade and the safest next action;
- no distributed/enterprise upgrade machinery before a real runtime requires it;
- keep recovery proportional to the actual risk.

## Explicitly out of scope

- Kubernetes rolling upgrades;
- Operator upgrades;
- multi-node leader/coordinator upgrades;
- cloud control-plane upgrades;
- OpenShift upgrade orchestration.

## Runtime-target upgrade compatibility

Upgrade/deprecation behavior must preserve the frozen deployment/runtime boundary.

A supported upgrade must not:

- move runtime-specific target/access settings into portable application intent;
- require users to copy credentials into application configuration;
- silently claim ownership of platform-managed resources;
- collapse previously distinct unsupported/unverifiable/authorization outcomes into generic failure.

If deployment/runtime state representation evolves, migration follows the same preflight -> migrate -> verify rules as other owned state.


## Acceptance

- [ ] Deployment/runtime target migrations preserve access secrecy and platform ownership boundaries.

- [ ] Supported upgrade paths have non-mutating preflight.
- [ ] Risky durable-state changes establish an appropriate recovery path first.
- [ ] Post-upgrade verification gates success.
- [ ] Rollback/recovery behavior is documented per migration class.
- [ ] Deprecated compatible input remains usable according to the published policy.
- [ ] New writers emit the canonical current representation.
- [ ] Upgrade/deprecation output is concise and actionable.
- [ ] Failure tests cover incompatible state, migration failure and verification failure.
- [ ] No later-runtime upgrade machinery is introduced speculatively.
- [ ] Validation follows `docs/DEVELOPMENT_GUIDELINES.md`.

Depends on: #175, #297, #298
Parent roadmap: #155


## Pre-release gate

Before creating this release:

- [ ] All acceptance criteria in this issue are complete.
- [ ] Required local/repository tests pass.
- [ ] The full relevant CI matrix has passed at least once on the **exact release-candidate commit**.
- [ ] Docker and Podman acceptance pass where applicable.
- [ ] Security, isolation and secret-leak checks pass where applicable.
- [ ] The documentation audit defined by #364 passes.
- [ ] Human-facing documentation matches the shipped behavior.
- [ ] Reference and normative specs match every changed public contract.
- [ ] No unresolved release blocker remains.
- [ ] Version, changelog, release notes and release metadata are consistent.
- [ ] Final exact-head acceptance evidence is recorded before tagging/releasing.

Acceptance answers whether the feature/release scope is complete. This gate answers whether the exact commit is safe and documented well enough to release.

Do not weaken or skip a required check merely to complete the release. Checks that are genuinely not applicable should be recorded as such rather than silently omitted.


## Provider Catalog upgrade and deprecation behavior

Upgrade/recovery rules also apply to provider catalog descriptors and resolved provider artifacts.

A provider upgrade must distinguish:

```text
catalog descriptor version
provider implementation version
Provider Protocol version
service/capability contract version
OCI artifact digest
product/engine version
```

These version axes must not be implicitly coupled.

Upgrade preflight must determine whether a new provider artifact/descriptor is compatible before replacing the currently resolved implementation.

Rules:

- digest changes are explicit artifact changes even when a mutable tag is unchanged;
- supported descriptor evolution prefers additive compatibility;
- deprecated catalog fields remain readable for the documented compatibility window and writers emit the canonical current form;
- provider replacement must preserve runtime/capability/delivery family semantics and ownership;
- rollback uses a previously verified provider/artifact identity only when technically safe;
- recovery diagnostics identify which boundary is incompatible: descriptor, protocol, contract, provider implementation or artifact identity.

### Provider catalog upgrade acceptance

- [ ] Provider artifact/digest changes are visible in upgrade preflight.
- [ ] Provider descriptor deprecations follow the published compatibility policy.
- [ ] A compatible provider patch/minor upgrade does not require portable application changes.
- [ ] An incompatible provider/protocol/contract combination fails before mutation with an actionable recovery path.
